newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Grain moves catch commodity markets' eye.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Grain moves catch commodity markets' eye.

text.p: The surprising volatility of grains prices caught the attention in otherwise routine commodity markets on Tuesday.

Dealers said the surge in Chicago soy prices was unexpected given high crop forecasts and put the rally down to spill-over buying from the nearby corn futures pit on the Chicago Board of Trade (CBOT) futures exchange.
"Corn is dragging beans up," a said one floor trader.
Corn futures registered limit gains in CBOT corn futures, turning round early forecasts for a downside day for the soy market, dealers said.

The U.S. Agriculture Department forecast the 1997/98 (September/August) soybean crop at 2.744 billion bushels. That figure was 15 percent higher than last year's output and above trade expectations for 2.607 billion to 2.731 billion.
Wheat futures were also boosted by the action in beans, but more directly a Jordanian purchase of 50,000 tonnes of U.S. hard red winter wheat fuelled early buying.
Consolidation in the U.S. dollar and a firmer tone in the U.S. stock and bond markets after their sell-off last Friday halted the nascent rally in gold.

The gold price hovered below the key $330.00 per ounce mark on Tuesday but dipped lower after New York opened, seemingly confirming dealers' opinion that failure to break into the $330s soon could signal another move to the downside.
Gold prices had rallied last Friday in response to a sharp decline in U.S. stock and bond markets.
But Wall Street's better performance on Monday diminished the chances that gold could summon up enough support to push higher for now, dealers said.
Gold closed at $326.35 in London, down $1.10 from Monday.
U.S. economic data due later this week could be a key for the gold price.

"Any signs that inflation is picking up will give the market further support...In any case there is no point getting too positive unless there is a convincing break of resistance at $330," brokers GNI said in a report.
Late trading on the London Metal Exchange was volatile, with copper and aluminium witnessing savage late movements prior to a mostly lower close for the complex.
At one stage it appeared as if prices were about to go into free fall as fund sales and dealer liquidation battered prices to late-afternoon lows, traders said.
But copper and aluminium in particular found some late buying, with the red metal actually ending modestly higher. Other metals, however, remained depressed and closed sharply lower.
"What happened this afternoon was that a lot of people who bought the dip at midday found there wasn't a bounce and just liquidated," one trader said.
Aluminium cascaded below $1,700 briefly, but was buttressed by chart-based support, and with copper rallying managed to close at $1,715, still $35 down from Monday.
LIFFE cocoa futures ended higher on technical considerations and the easier tone in sterling although volume was fairly light.

But coffee futures turned easier, having lost ground rapidly when the spot September contract fell through a psychological support level, while white sugar futures were very slow and slightly easier at $322.60.
